headline: Mackerel thick off Ocean Point, bass working the river mouths, groundfish holding deep in the bay
subhead: August's steady pattern is holding true to form — mackerel schools, staging bass, and pollock breaking the surface off the outer ledges.
body_markdown:
There's an old rule passed boat to boat around here every August, and it hasn't failed yet in forty years of watching it play out: when the mackerel show thick off Ocean Point and push into Linekin Bay, the bass aren't far behind, working the push of bait out of the Sheepscot and the Damariscotta on the back half of the tide. That rule is holding again this week, and it's about as reliable a read as this bay offers.

We flagged it two weeks back — called for a stable seasonal pattern to hold through the week — and that's exactly what's playing out. No big disruption, no cold-water shock, no southwest blow tearing up the surface. Just the bay doing its steady August business.

Mackerel are stacked thick in the usual pockets — off Ocean Point, inside Linekin Bay, and working the mouth of Boothbay Harbor itself on the morning tide. Small silver jigs — Swedish pimples, Kastmasters in the half-ounce range, or a plain string of mackerel flies dropped over the side — will load a bucket fast when the schools are up top, which tends to be early, before the sun gets high and pushes them down ten or fifteen feet. Anybody running a charter out of Boothbay this week ought to have bait covered inside the first half hour, and that bait is what's pulling the bass.

Striped bass are staging at the river mouths — the Sheepscot, the Damariscotta, the St. George down toward Port Clyde — sitting on the drop-offs and current seams where the outgoing tide funnels bait past them. This is a late-ebb bite more than anything else: let the water drain hard for a couple hours, then work soft-plastic jerkbaits or a bucktail with a white curl-tail trailer along the edges where the current breaks against the ledge. Bass in the twenty-six to thirty-two inch range have been the rule rather than the exception in this pattern, though the action is patchy — some stretches of river holding fish thick, others dead calm with nothing showing on the graph. That's the honest read: it's a good bite if you find the seam, and a slow afternoon if you don't.

Bluefish are the wildcard this far east. In a warm summer like this one, choppers have been known to push up past Muscle Ridge Channel and work the edges near Eastern Egg Rock, chasing the same bait the terns and puffins are diving on. If you see birds working hard and bass boats scattered wide instead of clustered tight, that's usually a sign blues have moved into the mix — switch to wire or heavier mono leader before you lose a whole tackle box to bite-offs.

Further out, the groundfish pattern is exactly where it should be for early August. Pollock are breaking the surface at dawn and again in the last hour of daylight over the outer ledges — Monhegan, White Island, the rips off Fisherman Island — and schoolie pollock in the two-to-five-pound range will hammer a small diamond jig worked with a fast, erratic retrieve just under the surface film. It's some of the most satisfying light-tackle fishing on this whole stretch of coast, and it costs nothing but a short run and a willingness to be out early.

Cod and haddock are holding true to form as well, sitting deep in the channels of Penobscot Bay — the water off Vinalhaven and down toward Isle au Haut, in that hundred-to-hundred-fifty-foot range where the bottom stays cool even when the surface warms up. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, worked vertically right on bottom with the current, are still the most consistent producer. This isn't a numbers fishery the way it was a generation back — anybody who's worked these grounds a long time will tell you the same — but a patient drift over the right piece of bottom on a slow tide still puts fish in the box, and the size classes have been respectable when you connect.

Monhegan itself remains the anchor of this whole pattern — bass working the ledges on the ebb, pollock stacked over the drop-offs, and the odd cod still holding in the deeper cuts around the island. It's a longer run than most are willing to make on a whim, but it's earned its reputation for a reason.

Looking ahead, there's nothing in the pattern that suggests a shakeup. If the wind stays out of the west and the tides keep running clean, expect the mackerel to hold in the same pockets, the bass to keep working the same river mouths on the same stage of tide, and the groundfish to sit right where they've been sitting. If a front pushes through and stirs the surface layer, the surface bite on pollock and mackerel will be the first to go quiet — that's when I'd shift attention to the deeper channel work and let the top-water settle back out before chasing it again.
